name: Kievan Rus'
title: Social Hierarchy of Kievan Rus': From Grand Prince to Kholop
period: c. 1016–1113 (from the Pravda of Yaroslav to the code of Vladimir Monomakh, the 11th century)

tiers.name: The grand prince of Kiev
tiers.you: You hold the throne of Kiev, take tribute from your brothers and nephews in the other cities and give the land its law, but every one of them is waiting for his turn, and some will not wait.
tiers.kid: The grand prince ruled from Kiev, gave the land its laws and collected tribute from the other princes.
tiers.rise: After Yaroslav’s death in 1054 no settled rule of succession took hold: the throne passed from elder to younger brother, from uncle to nephew and from father to son, and the princes fought over it. A defeat could cost a grand prince his city: after the Cumans beat the princes on the Alta River in 1068, Iziaslav fled to Poland to seek support and returned in a couple of years.
tiers.why: The grand prince of Kiev controlled the lands around the city, while his formally subordinate relatives ruled the other cities and paid him tribute.

tiers.name: Princes of the dynasty
tiers.you: You are a grandson of Yaroslav and prince of a minor town with a druzhina of your own, waiting for an uncle to die so that you may move to a richer city, and perhaps one day to Kiev.
tiers.kid: Princes of the same family ruled the other cities of Rus’ and hoped to move up, one day, to rule Kiev.
tiers.rise: Princely rank came only by birth into the dynasty, and a prince’s place in the order of seniority decided which city he could hope for. A prince could also lose his lands: by 1130 Mstislav the Great had exiled all the descendants of Vseslav of Polotsk to the Byzantine Empire.
tiers.why: Rurik’s descendants shared power over the land.

tiers.name: Boyars
tiers.you: You are a senior man of the prince’s druzhina: you sit in his council, command in his wars and run a town for him, and he rewards you with land, but your fortune lasts only as long as you and he keep faith with each other.
tiers.kid: Boyars were the prince’s chief warriors and advisers, and he rewarded them with land.
tiers.rise: A boyar’s standing came from service to a prince and from his family’s record of service, rewarded with offices and land. Because the bond was personal it could break: when Boris refused the throne of Kiev that his father’s druzhina offered him in 1015, the druzhina dispersed, and his brother Sviatopolk’s agents murdered him.
tiers.why: The boyars were the senior members of the prince’s druzhina and the highest nobility of Rus’, second only to the princes.

tiers.name: The junior druzhina and the prince's servants
tiers.term: otrok (soldier), tiun (privileged servant), mechnik (swordman), starosta (local official)
tiers.you: You are one of the prince’s “youths”: you ride in his bodyguard, eat at his feasts and help gather his tribute, and if you are killed on his land the community there must pay dearly for it.
tiers.kid: Young warriors guarded the prince, ate at his feasts and helped him collect tribute.
tiers.rise: A prince recruited where he could: free young warriors, Varangians hired for his wars, as Yaroslav brought them to Novgorod, and kholops, mainly house serfs, who filled the ranks of the princely servants, including the military.
tiers.why: Below the boyars stood the rank and file of the druzhina, the “youths” of the junior retinue, and the prince’s servants.

tiers.name: The clergy
tiers.you: You are a monk of the Monastery of the Caves at Kiev, favoured by the sons of Yaroslav, and you help keep the written record of the land in Cyrillic letters.
tiers.kid: Priests and monks served the new Christian Church, and churchmen wrote down the history of Rus’.
tiers.rise: Byzantine missionaries had come north in the 860s, and in 867 the Patriarch announced that the Rus’ had accepted a bishop; after 988 the princes patronized a local clergy and monks.
tiers.why: Christianity had long been known in these lands, but the Church as an order of its own dates from Vladimir’s baptism in about 987 and the baptism of Kiev he ordered in August 988.

tiers.name: Townspeople and merchants
tiers.you: You make glass vessels in a Kiev workshop; your wares go to towns from Suzdal to Beloozero, and the river fleets carry the furs and honey of Rus’ down the Dnieper to Constantinople.
tiers.kid: Townspeople made glassware and traded furs, honey and wax down the rivers as far as Constantinople.
tiers.rise: Trade made fortunes for merchants as for princes; debt could ruin a townsman, for a man sold for his debts became a kholop. After the Kiev riot of 1113 a new law limited the moneylenders’ interest.
tiers.why: The towns lived by trade and crafts.

tiers.name: Smerds
tiers.you: You grow grain and keep cattle in a village commune; you own what you farm and pay your own fines, but the law values your life no higher than a kholop’s and gives the prince your property when you die.
tiers.kid: Most people were farmers, called smerds, who grew grain and kept animals in village communities.
tiers.rise: Debt pulled smerds down: a peasant who took a loan became a zakup until he repaid it, and one sold for his debts became a kholop.
tiers.why: Most people of Rus’ were peasants: the Slavs were above all farmers, growing cereals and raising livestock.

tiers.name: Zakups
tiers.term: zakup (the bonded man, and the loan that bound him)
tiers.you: You took a loan, and until you repay it you live in dependence on the man who lent it; if you cannot, you may be sold for your debts and become a kholop.
tiers.kid: A zakup was a farmer who had borrowed money and was not free again until the debt was paid.
tiers.rise: Paying off the loan made a zakup free again; failing to pay could make him a kholop.
tiers.why: A zakup was a peasant who had taken a feudal loan, also called a zakup, and lived in dependence until he paid it off, when he became free again.

tiers.name: Kholops
tiers.you: You were taken captive and sold; your master may sell you again or hand you over for his debt, and the law asks of him only that he answer for what you do.
tiers.kid: Kholops were enslaved people: their masters owned them and could sell them.
tiers.rise: Capture, debt, crime or marriage made a free person a kholop. Some kholops, mainly house serfs, entered the princes’ service, among them their armed men.
tiers.why: Kholops were the unfree of Rus’: in the 11th and 12th centuries the word covered several kinds of dependent people, and especially slaves.
